newsitem.title: UK: IRAQ EXPORTS LOOM OVER N.SEA, MED CRUDE MARKETS.
newsitem.headline: IRAQ EXPORTS LOOM OVER N.SEA, MED CRUDE MARKETS.

text.p: North Sea crudes were steady in thin talk on Monday but set for further falls as cash Brent eased and looming Iraq exports pushed sellers to place late August barrels.

In the Mediterranean crude markets were split over future direction. While the flow of Iraqi barrels was expected to soften prices traders were hoping to place conveniently-sized and dated cargoes at good numbers.
"There are no (North Sea) grades moving but looking at the (Brent) curve the differentials really have to come under pressure," said a trader.
Sept Brent on the IPE gained eight cents to $18.56 a barrel by 1127 GMT, staging a modest recovery after dropping 42 cents on Friday, but cash market buyers were backing off.
"It's very difficult to get an idea of the market because there are very few interested bidders," said a trader.
The Sep/Oct intermonth spread was bid at -19 cents after trade on Friday at -17 cents. Oct/Nov was also seen easing a cents to -18/-14 cents.
Traders said news Iraq was planning to export 30 million barrels by the end of August was expected but could encourage sellers holding late month cargoes to accept lower numbers.
"This may prompt those with barrels left in August to move them sooner rather than later," said a trader.
North Forties was expected to lose ground from recent deals above Dated Brent +40 cents and Ekofisk and Statfjord could also ease.
"There's probably still an end month Forties left which certainly won't go for a premium with a four in front," said one.
Dated Brent was pegged unchanged at Sept Brent -30/-20 cents. Only one Aug 26-28 cargo was expected to turn wet on Monday.

Iraq's oil minister Amir Muhammed Rasheed said he anticipated 18 tankers to load 30 million barrels of oil by the end of August, with the first two million barrel shipment from Ceyhan in the next two days.
Rasheed said the oil tanker Arcadia anchored at Ceyhan on Monday and was awaiting approval of contracts by U.N. overseers before beginning to load.
Shipping brokers said last week that U.S. firm Coastal had fixed the VLCC Arcadia.

Seperately Russian oil sources said they would increase the amount of Iraqi crude they lift in the second six-month phase of the U.N.'s "oil-for-food" deal with Baghdad from the 28.54 million barrels bought in the first 180 days.
"Two deals were signed in Baghdad on Saturday," said Yuri Agababov, deputy general director of Zarubezhneft, the trading company coordinating Russian purchases.

He said Zarubezhneft would lift 5.55 million barrels and Alfa-Eko another 2.65 million barrels, while an additional two Russian firms would join the eight who lifted Kirkuk blend from December to May.
While it was generally recognised Iraqi exports will depress the discount against Dated Brent for Urals barrels towards the $1 mark, some traders saw short-term buoyancy.
An Italian trader bought an 80kt 19-20 loader Urals on Friday for -80 cents hoping to benefit from the lack of convenient alternatives for refiners looking in that date range.
"We know there is at lot of Kirkuk going trans-atlantic, with most loading on big ships into the third decade and we're convinced Urals will be competitive for a little longer," the trader said.
-- M.Thompson, S.Maguire +44 171 542 8060
